question: A 32-year-old man sustains a mid-shaft humeral fracture in a road traffic accident. On examination he cannot extend the wrist or fingers, and sensation is reduced over the dorsal first web space. Which nerve is injured and what is the CORRECT splint?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Ulnar nerve injury causes claw hand (ring and little fingers hyperextended at MCP, flexed at IP joints), not wrist drop. The anti-claw splint blocks MCP hyperextension. Wrist drop and dorsal first-web-space sensory loss point to the radial nerve.

Correct. The radial nerve winds around the spiral groove of the humerus and is vulnerable in mid-shaft fractures. Injury causes wrist drop (loss of wrist/finger extension) and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space. A cock-up (wrist extension) splint keeps the wrist at ~30° extension to maintain hand function while awaiting recovery.
Median nerve injury causes loss of thenar opposition, 'ape hand' deformity, and sensory loss over the lateral 3½ digits (palmar). Wrist drop is not a feature of median nerve injury.
Common peroneal nerve injury causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion and eversion), not wrist drop. An AFO is the correct splint for foot drop. The nerve is not at risk in humeral shaft fractures.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the nerve-fracture-deficit-splint chain: Radial/mid-humerus→wrist drop→cock-up; Ulnar/medial epicondyle→claw hand→anti-claw; Common peroneal/fibular head→foot drop→AFO.
Correct. Radial nerve + mid-shaft humerus fracture = wrist drop + dorsal first web space loss → cock-up splint.
